body: On a typical commercial flight, airline pilots spend only a small proportion of their time physically controlling the aircraft. Pilots normally hand-fly takeoff and part of the initial climb, while the autopilot handles most of the flight until approach. According to a 2026 report by the International Air Transport Association (IATA), commercial aircraft operate with automation engaged for approximately 90% of the time. On a long-haul flight, a pilot may spend just a few minutes controlling a Boeing 787 or Airbus A350, although operating procedures and weather conditions can influence this substantially.

Airborne manual flying normally starts with takeoff, which remains a pilot-controlled maneuver on conventional commercial airplanes. The pilot maintains directional control, rotates, and establishes the initial climb, and the autopilot can only be engaged once the aircraft has reached its approved minimum engagement height. After departure, the crew can generally engage the autopilot relatively early, sometimes only a few hundred feet above the ground. According to IATA's 2020 Aircraft Handling and Manual Flying Skills Report, many surveyed pilots reported engaging it around 400 or 500 feet above ground level, while others preferred to continue flying manually through 5,000 or even 10,000 feet. On arrival, the final flare and touchdown are normally performed manually, although suitably equipped aircraft can also carry out automatic landings under the appropriate conditions.

Estimates differ substantially. Back in 2011, airline captain Rory Kay, co-chair of a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) advisory committee on pilot training, said pilots were using automation “for all but approximately three minutes of a flight”. Another committee member, captain Bob Coffman, estimated that pilots at commuter airlines might fly with the autopilot disengaged for approximately 80 seconds during a typical two-hour flight. Airline pilot Spencer Marker said most airline pilots spend ten minutes or less manually controlling their aircraft. Ten minutes represents almost 17% of a one-hour flight, but only 1.7% of a ten-hour service.

Airline policies determine how much manual flying is allowed. IATA's 2020 survey received 5,650 responses overall; only 36% of the 5,241 pilots answering the relevant question said their airline allowed and supported manual flying without limitations, and approximately 37% of 3,452 respondents admitted hesitating to disengage the autopilot. A 2017 study of more than 1,500 commercial pilots found only 35.5% of long-haul pilots agreed they had sufficient opportunities to hand-fly, compared with 79.9% of pilots operating short- and medium-haul flights. Among pilots in supportive procedural environments, 68% felt they had sufficient opportunities to maintain manual flying skills, falling to 26% where airlines imposed more restrictive procedures.

Regulators have raised concerns for well over a decade. The Associated Press reported in 2011 that a draft FAA study examined 46 accidents and major incidents and found problems involving manual aircraft handling or automated flight controls in more than 60% of the accidents and 30% of the major incidents reviewed. The FAA issued Safety Alert for Operators 13002 in 2013 encouraging airlines to provide manual flying opportunities, and a further safety alert in 2017 called for manual flying proficiency to be reinforced through training and normal line operations. In its 2026 flight path management report, IATA identified manual handling as an important safety concern, and research found nearly 80% of surveyed pilots disagreed that simulator training alone was sufficient to maintain manual flying skills.
en.summary: According to a 2026 IATA report, commercial aircraft fly with automation engaged for about 90% of the time; pilots usually hand-fly only takeoff and approach — sometimes just minutes on a long-haul flight — but autopilot does not mean the aircraft flies unsupervised.
en.title: Here's How Much Of A Flight Airline Pilots Actually Hand-Fly

body: 在典型的民航航班上，機師實際手動操控飛機的時間只占很小一部分。機師通常手動執行起飛與部分初始爬升，隨後由自動駕駛接手大部分航程，直至進場階段。根據國際航空運輸協會（IATA）2026年報告，民航機約90%的時間處於自動化飛行狀態；在長程航班上，機師操控波音787或空中巴士A350的時間可能僅數分鐘，實際長短取決於操作程序與天氣狀況。

手動飛行通常自起飛開始。起飛在傳統民航機上仍由機師操控，機師保持方向控制、拉起機頭並建立初始爬升；自動駕駛須待飛機到達核准的最低接通高度後才能接通。離場後，機組通常可於離地僅數百英尺時接通自動駕駛；根據IATA 2020年《飛機操控與手動飛行技能報告》，許多受訪機師表示約在400或500英尺接通自動駕駛，也有人選擇手動飛至5000甚至10000英尺。進場時，機師可能在目視進場提早解除自動駕駛，或保持接通至落地前不久；最後拉平與觸地通常仍由人工執行。

實際數字因人而異。2011年，美國聯邦航空總署（FAA）機師訓練諮詢委員會共同主席、機長羅里·凱伊表示，機師在飛行中幾乎全程使用自動化，僅約3分鐘例外；同委員會成員、機長鮑勃·科夫曼則估計，通勤航空公司的機師在典型2小時航班中，自動駕駛解除的時間約80秒。另一名機師斯賓塞·馬克則表示，多數機師手動操控的時間在10分鐘以內。航班長短影響甚大：10分鐘在1小時航班中占近17%，在10小時航班中僅占1.7%。

航空公司政策決定機師有多少手動飛行機會。IATA 2020年調查共收到5650份回覆，其中回答相關問題的5241名機師中，僅36%表示其航空公司無限制地允許並支持手動飛行；另一題3452份回覆中，約37%承認即使程序允許，仍會猶豫是否解除自動駕駛。2017年一項調查訪問逾1500名民航機師，僅35.5%的長程機師認為自己有足夠手動飛行機會，短中程機師則為79.9%；在程序環境友善的航空公司，68%的機師認為有足夠機會維持手動飛行技能，在限制較多的航空公司則僅26%。

監管機關長期關注此議題。美聯社2011年報導，一份FAA草案研究檢視46起事故與重大事件，發現逾60%的事故與30%的重大事件涉及手動操控或自動飛行控制問題；FAA隨後於2013年發布營運人安全警示SAFO 13002，鼓勵航空公司提供手動飛行機會，2017年再發警示要求透過訓練與日常營運強化手動飛行熟練度。IATA在2026年航路管理報告中亦將手動操控列為重要安全關切，並指出近80%的受訪機師不同意僅靠模擬機訓練足以維持手動飛行技能。
zh.summary: 根據國際航空運輸協會2026年報告，民航機約90%的時間以自動化飛行；機師通常只在起飛與進場階段手動操控，長程航班上可能僅數分鐘，但自動駕駛並不等於無人監督。
zh.title: 民航機師實際手動飛行的時間有多少？
